title: Why Is My Houseplant Not Growing?

content_html:
A houseplant can grow very slowly because of low light, season, crowded roots, poor watering, or a true nutrient limitation. Before fertilizing, check whether the plant is healthy and whether basic conditions support growth; feeding stressed roots can make the problem worse.

Separate slow growth from an unhealthy plant

If leaves and stems remain firm and well colored, a seasonal pause may be normal. Yellowing, leaf drop, soft tissue, or pests indicate that stress or disease should be addressed before expecting new growth.

Check whether the plant receives enough light

A plant can survive in low light without having enough energy to make new leaves. Consider actual useful light hours and distance from the window; move it gradually if more light is needed to avoid sunburn from a sudden change.

Check roots, pot size, and drainage

A dense root mass, water racing through immediately, or a pot that stays waterlogged can limit growth. Repot only when there is a clear reason and use an appropriate pot size and mix rather than moving straight to an oversized container.

Fertilize only when light and roots can use it

Fertilizer cannot replace light or root aeration. If the plant is actively growing and the species benefits from feeding, use the label dose; excess salts can burn roots and slow growth further.
